citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China, Meituan Group)
description: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) is a benchmark dataset for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about objects in images (e.g., "Is there a car in the image?"). POPE supports three sampling strategies — Random, Popular, and Adversarial — to probe whether LVLMs hallucinate frequently appearing or co-occurring objects.
name: POPE
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth objects are obtained from existing human annotations in MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA. For unannotated datasets, automatic segmentation via SEEM is used. Questions are formulated using the template "Is there a/an <object> in the image?" with binary Yes/No answers. Negative objects are sampled under Random, Popular, or Adversarial strategies, maintaining a 1:1 ratio of positive to negative questions per image.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is built on MSCOCO, which has an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part. This is intentionally exploited in the Popular and Adversarial sampling strategies to probe LVLMs' tendency to hallucinate frequently appearing or co-occurring objects. The 1:1 ratio of positive to negative questions is designed to mitigate label imbalance bias in evaluation.
rai:dataCollection: POPE is constructed from existing image datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA). For each image, ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. Negative (nonexistent) objects are sampled using three strategies: Random (random sampling of absent objects), Popular (top-k most frequent objects in the dataset that are absent from the image), and Adversarial (top-k objects that most frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects but are absent from the image). The ratio of ground-truth to nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance. For MSCOCO evaluation, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects were randomly selected, with 6 questions constructed per image.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations from MSCOCO validation set, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. MSCOCO provides human-labeled object annotations covering 80 object categories from the segmentation challenge.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataLimitations: POPE only evaluates coarse-grained object hallucination and does not cover fine-grained hallucinations such as object number, attributes, or positions. The evaluation uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No responses, leading to inaccurate results. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, the object label set may be inconsistent with human annotations, causing divergence in evaluation results. Results may be affected by the data distribution of the sampled subset due to computational resource limitations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative sampling strategies are applied to construct evaluation questions: (1) Random Sampling — randomly sample objects absent from the image; (2) Popular Sampling — select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that are absent from the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling — rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k absent ones. The ratio of positive to negative questions is fixed at 1:1 for label balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For MSCOCO, only the 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge are considered. Images are filtered to include only those with more than 3 ground-truth objects. For CHAIR metric computation, human-crafted parsing rules are applied to extract predicted objects from generated captions. For SEEM-based annotation, segmentation results replace human annotations as the source of ground-truth objects.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world deployments. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect understanding of the external environment could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The paper also notes that hallucinations can harm user experiences in applications such as image captioning for blind users.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs); benchmarking the tendency of LVLMs to generate objects inconsistent with the target image; probing whether LVLMs hallucinate frequently appearing or co-occurring objects; extending hallucination evaluation to unannotated datasets via automatic segmentation tools.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) — an automatic segmentation tool used to annotate objects in images from datasets without existing annotations (A-OKVQA, GQA, and optionally MSCOCO). ChatGPT was also used to assist in parsing open-ended VQA responses for evaluation.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper specifies 6 questions per image (l=6) but this is the number of polling questions, not independent annotations per item in the traditional sense; the paper does not describe multiple independent human annotations per question.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: No human annotators were used for POPE itself; ground-truth labels come from existing dataset annotations (MSCOCO) or automatic segmentation (SEEM).
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality analysis is described; labels are derived from existing annotations or automatic tools.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No annotation platform (e.g., MTurk) is used; annotations come from existing datasets or automated segmentation tools.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No data collection timeframe is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of object-level image annotations; no personal or sensitive information is collected or discussed.
null_reasons.license: No license is mentioned in the paper, and the HuggingFace dataset card for lmms-lab/POPE does not specify a license.
